slides.say: The circumference of the smaller circle is ten pi centimeters, and the shaded area, inside the larger circle but outside the smaller one, is thirty-nine pi square centimeters. Between which two values is the circumference of the larger circle, in centimeters?
at: The circumference of the smaller circle

slides.say: We need the circumference of the large circle, so we need its radius. [short pause] We'll go from the small circle to the large one, one given at a time.

[short pause] Let's start with the first given. The circumference of the small circle is ten pi. If we know a circle's circumference, can we find its radius? Yes. The circumference is two pi r, so two pi r equals ten pi.
at: so two pi r equals ten pi
so two pi r equals ten pi

slides.say: We can cancel pi on both sides, so two r is ten. Two radii make a diameter, so the diameter is ten. So the radius is ten divided by two, five. That's the radius of the small circle.
at: So the radius is ten divided by two
So the radius is ten divided by two

slides.say: Now its area. The area of a circle is pi r squared. Pi times five squared is twenty-five pi. That's the area of the small white circle.

On to the second given. The shaded ring is thirty-nine pi. The ring and the white circle together make the whole large circle. So the area of the large circle is twenty-five pi plus thirty-nine pi, which is sixty-four pi.
at: The shaded ring is thirty-nine pi
So the area of the large circle

slides.say: If we know the area, we can find the radius. Pi R squared is sixty-four pi. Cancel pi, and R squared is sixty-four. So R is eight, because eight squared is sixty-four. Let's remember that.
at: Pi R squared is sixty-four pi

slides.say: [pause] Now let's see what they asked. The circumference of the large circle. Two pi R is two pi times eight, which is sixteen pi.
at: Now let's see what they asked
The circumference of the large circle
Two pi R is two pi times eight

slides.say: But sixteen pi isn't in the choices. The choices are ranges, so they want us to estimate. How much is pi? Its digits go on forever, three point one four one five nine, and so on. So pi is more than three point one four, and less than three point one five.
at: So pi is more than three point one four

slides.say: First the lower end, sixteen times three point one four. Sixteen times three is forty-eight. Now sixteen times point one four. Point one four is fourteen hundredths, so we work out sixteen times fourteen, and then make it hundredths. Sixteen times fourteen is two hundred twenty-four, so it's two point two four.
at: Sixteen times fourteen is two hundred

slides.say: Together, fifty point two four. So sixteen pi is more than fifty point two four. Now let's find the upper end. Sixteen times point one five is two point four. So sixteen times three point one five is fifty point four.
at: So sixteen times three point one five

slides.say: So sixteen pi is between fifty point two four and fifty point four. That's between fifty and fifty-one. Choice number four is our answer.
at: Choice number four is our answer

slides.say: Careful with the trap. If you round pi down to three, you get exactly forty-eight, and choice number one looks right. Here that's too rough. The point one four adds more than two. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: If you round pi down to three
